Volume 14 · Chapter 04

Search, matching and labor dynamics

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v14-c03

By the endDerive dynamic labor-market equilibria and evaluate their implications.

Volume 14 · Chapter 4

Jobs are created through a market, not by a flow identity alone

A decline in unemployment can reflect faster hiring, fewer separations or a change in who searches. A firm opens a vacancy only if the expected value of a filled job covers recruiting costs. That value depends on the wage, and the wage depends on workers’ alternatives. This chapter closes that loop, then asks whether the resulting allocation maximizes discounted social surplus.

Capability. Derive a continuous-time matching equilibrium with an explicit information and financing structure; prove its stationary existence and uniqueness; calculate transitional unemployment after a permanent shock; and verify a constrained-efficient allocation rather than infer efficiency from low unemployment. All quantities below are original synthetic examples, not a calibration to current labor data.

Prerequisites. Incomplete markets and heterogeneous agents distinguishes a distribution from an individual state. Dynamic optimization supplies value verification and controlled remainders; stochastic growth separates equilibrium mechanisms from empirical validation. The discrete-period flows in labor markets remain useful, but their probabilities are not the continuous-time rates introduced here.

1. States, matching and the unit of time

A fixed labor force has mass one. At time t its unemployment share is u(t), employment is 1−u(t), and vacancies per member of the labor force are v(t). Only unemployed workers search; each employed worker fills one job. There is no participation margin, worker heterogeneity or on-the-job search. A continuum law of large numbers is a maintained aggregation assumption: individual transitions are random, while aggregate shares obey deterministic flow equations conditional on common primitives.

Time is continuous. A hazard λ has units of inverse time: the probability of its event in a short interval dt is λdt+o(dt), with two or more events contributing o(dt). It is not a probability over a whole year. A constant hazard has survival probability H(t) satisfying H′=−λH, H(0)=1, hence H(t)=exp(−λt). Its mean waiting time is integral_0^infinity H(t)dt=1/λ when λ>0.

m(u,v)=A u^α v^(1−α),   A>0,   0<α<1;   θ=v/u;   f(θ)=Aθ^(1−α),   q(θ)=Aθ^(−α).

Here m is matches per unit time per labor-force member, θ is vacancies per unemployed worker, f=m/u is the worker job-finding hazard and q=m/v is the vacancy-filling hazard. The matching elasticity with respect to unemployment is α and with respect to vacancies is 1−α. Holding the other pool fixed, more searchers improve vacancy filling and more vacancies improve job finding; holding their ratio fixed, scaling both pools scales matches proportionately. This is a stipulated constant-returns technology, not a proof that observed matching has constant returns.

Each filled job separates at exogenous hazard s>0. For u>0,v>0, f=θq. At v=0 set m=f=0; do not evaluate q at θ=0. At u=0 there are no searching workers and m=0. Under positive separation, the boundary u=0 immediately has positive unemployment inflow. The flow equation is

u′(t)=s[1−u(t)]−m(u(t),v(t))=s−[s+f(θ(t))]u(t).

For constant finite θ, solve this linear equation by multiplying by exp((s+f)t). The result is u(t)=u*+[u(0)−u*]exp(−(s+f)t), where u*=s/(s+f). It stays in [0,1] and converges monotonically to its unique stationary share. These are aggregate dynamics and not an assertion that any one worker stops switching jobs.

The two-state worker transition probabilities over an interval Δ must allow repeated moves. Starting unemployed means u(0)=1 for that worker’s state probability, giving P(U→E)=f[1−exp(−(s+f)Δ)]/(s+f). Starting employed gives P(E→U)=s[1−exp(−(s+f)Δ)]/(s+f). The probability of at least one finding before leaving an uninterrupted unemployment spell is instead 1−exp(−fΔ). Occupancy at the end of an interval is a different event.

Worked case 1: a hazard can exceed one

Take (f,s)=(1,1/10), and choose Δ so exp(−(f+s)Δ)=1/2, namely Δ=10log(2)/11. The exact transition probabilities are (P(U→E),P(E→U))=(5/11,1/22). Their stationary unemployment share is 1/11, agreeing with flow balance. Neither endpoint probability equals its hazard times Δ exactly.

Later we will obtain f=2. That is a legitimate continuous-time intensity. Reusing f as a one-year probability would give two and an invalid transition row. Continuous-time matching can generate repeated transitions within a year; the instantaneous flow is not a count of distinct people hired over that year. When s=0, the endpoint finding formula reduces to 1−exp(−fΔ), as it should.

2. Ownership, finance, values and bargaining

A filled job produces a flow y>0 of the numeraire and pays its worker wage flow w. An unemployed worker obtains real home-production or leisure utility b≥0 in the same transferable-utility scale. It is not an unemployment-insurance transfer. Each open vacancy costs κ>0 per unit time in recruiting services. Agents are risk neutral and discount flow utility at constant rate r>0, so a value is an expected integral of exp(−rt) times flows. A wage has units of goods per time; a job value has units of goods.

Jobs and recruiting firms belong to diversified private owners. Owners pay recruiting bills from their own wealth or enforceable credit claims and receive net firm returns; workers receive wages. The model explicitly assumes frictionless risk-neutral financing of the finite present-value recruiting plans considered here, without a borrowing or cash-in-advance constraint. No outside grant is added to firm values. Recruiting costs remain real costs in consolidated welfare, and financial transfers cancel. For our cases we also exhibit sufficient owned reserves to prefinance recruiting without relying on prospective hiring receipts. A model with limited working capital needs new state variables and entry conditions.

A vacancy is a position incurring a running cost until it fills; opening or closing it has no additional lump-sum cost. Its owner may choose not to enter. On separation a firm can return to the vacancy option. Let U,E denote worker values in unemployment and employment, and V,J the values of an open vacancy and a filled job. Individual pairs take market hazards and outside options as given; aggregate entry determines those hazards. For a stationary market, condition on the first dt, use exp(−r dt)=1−r dt+o(dt), subtract the current value and divide by dt. Bounded constant flows and finite hazards justify the limiting equations:

rU=b+f(E−U),   rE=w+s(U−E),
rV=−κ+q(J−V),   rJ=y−w+s(V−J).

The same equations can be checked directly by integrating discounted expected flows of the two-state chains. If a bounded vector satisfies them, multiplying its value along the chain by exp(−rt), integrating conditional increments and taking expectations leaves its discounted terminal value. That term vanishes since r>0 and the vector is bounded. Thus these equations identify actual expected values, not an arbitrary solution to an asset equation.

Free entry. With positive vacancies, V=0: positive V invites more entry, while an entrant need not accept negative V. The vacancy equation then gives κ=qJ. This is zero net present value of an entry opportunity, not zero recruiting expenditure and not J=0. For an inactive market use a no-profitable-entry inequality; do not divide by an undefined filling rate.

Pair-specific Nash bargaining. At a meeting, either side can refuse. Conditional on positive total surplus, they choose a constant wage to maximize (E_i−U)^η(J_i−V)^(1−η), where 0<η<1 is the worker bargaining weight. Hold the outside values U,V and the aggregate market fixed while varying this pair’s wage. In the active equilibrium V=0, (r+s)E_i=w_i+sU and (r+s)J_i=y−w_i. Therefore the worker surplus X_i=E_i−U=(w_i−rU)/(r+s) increases one-for-one with the firm surplus decrease; their sum S_i=(y−rU)/(r+s) is independent of w_i.

For fixed S>0, maximize ηlog X+(1−η)log(S−X) on 0<X<S. Its second derivative is strictly negative and the objective tends to −∞ at both ends; the unique global optimum is X=ηS and J=(1−η)S. This derivation differentiates a pair’s own wage, not an equilibrium wage formula in which U would move with aggregate wages. Subtracting and adding the market value equations now gives

S=(y−b)/(r+s+ηf),   E−U=ηS,   J=(1−η)S,
rU=b+fηS,   w=ηy+(1−η)b+ηκθ.

For the last expression, use w=rU+(r+s)ηS and κθ=f(1−η)S. The outside option is U, which includes future opportunities; replacing it with the flow b would discard that continuation benefit. Wages transfer surplus between owners and workers, while recruiting uses real resources.

3. Close the equilibrium and prove the boundaries

Define an active stationary equilibrium as finite θ>0, constant wage and bounded values satisfying the four value equations, pairwise surplus bargaining, free entry, and u*=s/(s+f), v*=θu*. All primitives A,κ,r,s are strictly positive, α,η lie in (0,1), and first suppose y>b. Substitution reduces the entire system to

H(θ) ≡ κ[(r+s)θ^α/A+ηθ] − (1−η)(y−b)=0.

Existence and uniqueness. H is continuous on [0,infinity), H(0)<0, H(θ)→infinity, and for θ>0 its derivative κ[(r+s)αθ^(α−1)/A+η] is strictly positive. The intermediate value theorem gives exactly one positive root. At this root construct f,q,S,X,J,U,E,w from the preceding formulas; S,X,J are positive, u*∈(0,1), v*>0, and direct substitution verifies every value equation and κ=qJ. In particular y−w=(r+s)J>0 and w−b=(r+s+f)X>0. This constructs an equilibrium rather than assuming one. Conversely every active equilibrium must satisfy H=0, so the construction is complete in the declared stationary domain.

At a no-vacancy boundary, define an entry test by vanishing positive vacancy masses, so q tends to infinity while an individual worker’s finding rate tends to zero. If y>b, such nonentry cannot persist. With U=b/r, let Vhat be a prospective entrant’s continuing vacancy value. Pair bargaining gives Jhat−Vhat=(1−η)(y−b−rVhat)/(r+s); substituting into rVhat=−κ+q(Jhat−Vhat) yields rVhat=[q(1−η)(y−b)−κ(r+s)]/[r+s+q(1−η)], positive for sufficiently large finite q. This contradicts no profitable entry. The limiting-entry convention is part of the boundary specification; q is never assigned a finite value at zero vacancies.

If y≤b, no positive root exists because H(θ)>0 for θ>0. The stationary inactive allocation u=1,v=0 has U=b/r and no mutually beneficial new match. To make both parties weakly accept with V=0 requires w≥rU=b and w≤y; this is impossible for y<b and yields zero surplus only at equality. A zero-surplus meeting cannot pay positive recruiting cost. Nonentry is therefore consistent. At θ=0,q’s formal limit is infinite, but that is no license to multiply infinity by zero: no vacancy is operated and the agreement/entry inequalities give the boundary directly. Transitions after a shock that makes old matches unviable require closure and renegotiation rules; our shock exercise stays in y>b. Cases with zero recruiting cost, zero separation, endpoint elasticities or no discounting are outside this theorem.

Computation. Bracket the unique root by starting at θ=0 and doubling a positive upper endpoint until H is nonnegative; H→infinity proves eventual bracketing. Bisect and preserve opposite weak signs. After n bisections the root remains in an interval of original width divided by 2^n, so its midpoint error is at most half that width. Report this bracket or a residual bound, not only a solver’s “success” flag. Since H′≥κη, any positive candidate θhat has |θhat−θ*|≤|H(θhat)|/(κη) by the mean-value theorem. This bound is valid but can be loose. When α=1/2, x=√θ reduces H to an ordinary quadratic with exactly one positive root.

Worked case 2: reconcile the whole stationary market

Use (A,α,η,r,s,κ,b,y)=(1,1/2,1/2,1/10,1/10,1/2,1/5,9/10). Write x=√θ. The entry equation is (1/4)x²+(1/10)x−7/20=0, or 5x²+2x−7=0. Its only positive root is one, hence (θ,f,q)=(1,1,1). The surplus, worker gain and firm value are (S,X,J)=(1,1/2,1/2), and the wage and worker values are (w,U,E)=(4/5,7,15/2).

The stock and flow quantities are (u*,v*,m*)=(1/11,1/11,1/11). Job losses s(1−u*) and matches m* are equal. Free entry reads (1/2)=1·(1/2). Each employed firm receives 9/10, pays 4/5 and earns 1/10 until separation; J=(1/10)/(r+s)=1/2. A vacancy costs 1/2 per unit time while open, even though its net value is zero.

Recruiting costs in the stationary economy are κv*=1/22 per unit time. An owned risk-free reserve 5/11 earning r=1/10 can cover that entire recruiting flow forever, before using any firm receipt. The reserve is an existing owner asset, not part of match surplus and not new output. Its cost is not counted again after recruiting expenses have been subtracted.

The consolidated real flow y(1−u*)+bu*−κv* is 87/110. Wages cancel between workers and firms. Aggregating unemployed values U and employed worker-plus-firm values E+J gives 87/11; multiplying by r reproduces the steady flow. This accounting does not imply a planner optimum until the welfare comparison below is proved.

4. Productivity shocks: jumps in offers, gradual changes in employment

Implicit differentiation of H=0, with other primitives fixed, gives dθ/dy=(1−η)/H′>0 and dθ/db=−(1−η)/H′<0. Also dθ/dκ<0 and dθ/dr=dθ/ds<0. Raising η lowers θ because ∂H/∂η=κθ+(y−b)>0. Increasing A raises θ since ∂H/∂A=−κ(r+s)θ^α/A²<0. These are structural comparative statics, not identified causal estimates.

For a productivity increase, f increases, q decreases, and u*=s/(s+f) decreases. The wage rises because dw/dy=η+ηκ(dθ/dy)>0. Since v*=sθ/(s+Aθ^(1−α)), its derivative with respect to θ is s[s+αf]/(s+f)²>0: more vacancies coexist with lower unemployment. A change in s moves both the entry equation and the flow-balance curve; it cannot be treated solely as a movement along a fixed Beveridge curve.

Now let productivity change unexpectedly and permanently at time zero, remaining above b. Existing wages are immediately renegotiated by the same Nash rule; vacancies can adjust without installation delays; no other state or financing constraint is added. After the news, θ,w and the individual continuation values jump to the new stationary-market values. The unemployed share cannot jump because transition hazards are finite. At each later u, firms choose v=θnew u, keeping the same filling rate; workers’ future hazards therefore do not depend on the current aggregate stock. The exact path is the preceding linear transition with fnew.

Do not apply this shortcut to an anticipated, temporary or recurrent productivity process. With deterministic changing future values the equations instead include time derivatives, for example rJ=y−w−sJ+J′ and rU=b+f(E−U)+U′ in an active market. With common Markov shocks, conditional future-state terms replace these derivatives. Expectations then enter job values and current entry. Computing a sequence of unrelated stationary equilibria omits those terms.

Worked case 3: a permanent shock and a nonstationary observation

Start at the baseline steady state and raise y to 13/5. The new root and values are (θ,f,q,S,w,U,E,J)=(4,2,1/2,2,12/5,22,23,1). Long-run unemployment is 1/21, but immediately it remains 1/11 and vacancies jump to 4/11. The response is

u(t)=1/21+(1/11−1/21)exp(−21t/10),   v(t)=4u(t).

At the half-gap date t=10log(2)/21 the levels and unemployment derivative are (u,v,m,u′)=(16/231,64/231,32/231,-1/22). Treating this observation as a steady state would infer f=s(1−u)/u=43/32, although the true hazard is two. The missing term is −u′/u in f=[s(1−u)−u′]/u.

Along this transition v(t)≤4/11, so an owned reserve 20/11 earning r covers the maximum recruiting flow forever. The exact discounted recruiting expenditure is smaller: integrating κ·4u(t) gives 120/121. These reserve amounts are sufficient prefunding demonstrations, not equilibrium capital requirements or unrecorded gifts.

5. A discounted planner comparison and the Hosios condition

For the planner analysis maintain y>b. Keep the same matching technology, exogenous separation, labor force and real outside benefit b. The planner cannot instantly match workers. It chooses nonnegative finite tightness θ(t), with v(t)=θ(t)u(t), to maximize

∫_0^infinity exp(−rt){y[1−u(t)]+bu(t)−κθ(t)u(t)}dt,
subject to u′=s−[s+f(θ)]u,   u(0)=u0∈[0,1].

Admissible controls are measurable and locally bounded and have finite discounted recruiting expenditure; they use the same financing authority as the market. The linear state equation then has a unique absolutely continuous solution in [0,1], as its integrating-factor formula shows. Positive production/home-utility flows are bounded, so the discounted objective exists. Controls with infinite discounted cost have value −∞ and cannot improve on a finite-cost candidate. This is consolidated worker-and-owner surplus in a common scale; it is neither frictionless first best nor an assertion that every individual benefits.

We will verify a value function directly rather than presume a general optimal-control theorem. Seek W(u)=a−Du, where D>0 is the social value of converting unemployment into employment. For any θ, the instantaneous reward plus W′ times state drift is

y−sD+u{b−y+sD−κθ+Df(θ)}.

For D>0, the θ-dependent expression g(θ)=DAθ^(1−α)−κθ is strictly concave on θ>0, has positive infinite right slope at zero and tends to −∞ at infinity. Its unique global maximum satisfies κ=D(1−α)q(θ). Require the Bellman equality rW=reward+W′u′ at this maximizing constant θP. Matching constant and u coefficients gives

D=(y−b)/(r+s+αf(θP)),   κ=(1−α)q(θP)D,
κ[(r+s)θP^α/A+αθP]=(1−α)(y−b),   a=(y−sD)/r.

The root exists uniquely by the same continuous-monotone argument as for H. Thus all proposed coefficients are finite. For every u∈[0,1] and every feasible θ, global maximization of g proves rW(u)≥reward(u,θ)+W′(u)u′. Along any admissible control, the chain rule for an absolutely continuous state gives

∫_0^T exp(−rt)reward(t)dt ≤ W(u0)−exp(−rT)W(u(T)).

Because W is bounded on [0,1], the last term vanishes. Equality holds for θP at all times; its costs are bounded and integrable. This proves optimality over all admissible time-varying controls from the same initial unemployment, not only over constant policies or their steady-state flows. For u0>0, the state stays positive at finite dates; strict concavity of g means an optimal control equals θP almost everywhere. For u0=0, immediate separation makes u(t)>0 for t>0, so the same assertion holds except at a single irrelevant initial instant.

Decentralization. The market equation becomes exactly the planner equation when η=α. Conversely, solve the market root equation for the bargaining weight at a given positive θ:

η=[(y−b)−κ(r+s)θ^α/A]/[(y−b)+κθ].

The denominator is positive, so a given positive θ can correspond to at most one η. At θP that value is α; therefore the market allocation is constrained efficient if and only if η=α in this specified model. This is the Hosios condition: the worker surplus share equals the unemployment elasticity of matching. If η<α, the earlier comparative static gives θmarket>θP and excessive recruiting; if η>α, entry is too low. The criterion uses marginal matching contributions, not a presumption that workers should receive half of output.

If b were an insurance payment financed by taxes, it would enter individual incentives but would cancel with the taxpayers’ transfer in consolidated resources; any real leisure component and tax distortions would require separate terms. Similarly, heterogeneous matches, recruiting technologies without constant returns, participation, borrowing limits or endogenous separation alter the planner problem. The displayed equality is not a universal welfare test for every matching market.

Worked case 4: lower unemployment can come with lower surplus

The baseline has α=η=1/2, so θP=1,D=1,a=8 and W(u)=8−u. Change only the bargaining weight to 1/3. The entry equation in x=√θ becomes 5x²+3x−14=0, whose positive root is 7/5. The distorted-market quantities are (θ,f,u*,w,S,J)=(49/25,7/5,1/15,19/25,21/20,7/10). Unemployment is lower than 1/11, but the higher recruiting intensity is not efficient.

For any fixed tightness θ, solve its own affine evaluation equation: Dθ=(y−b+κθ)/(r+s+f), aθ=(y−sDθ)/r, and Wθ(u)=aθ−Dθu. This is the exact discounted reward along that rule, justified by the same bounded remainder. For the distorted rule, (aθ,Dθ)=(159/20,21/20).

Compare both policies from the same initial u0=1/11. Their values are (W(u0),Wθ(u0),loss)=(87/11,432/55,3/55). Comparing each policy’s steady flow from a different initial state would not be this welfare experiment. The gain is aggregate; changing wage bargaining redistributes rents between workers and owners, and no Pareto improvement follows without a feasible compensating transfer.

6. Calibration, identification and what the model leaves out

In a stationary two-state economy, observed u and a separately measured s identify f=s(1−u)/u within the model. If vacancies are measured on the same population basis, θ=v/u is observed too. That does not identify every matching primitive: log f=log A+(1−α)log θ is one equation for A and α. With the baseline θ=1,f=1, every α∈(0,1) fits with A=1. All other baseline values also fit because only the level of f and q at θ=1 enters their equations. The entry condition can pin down η=1/2 if κ,r,s,y,b are genuinely known, but it cannot then establish η=α from this one observation.

Across markets or dates, stable A and genuine variation in log θ could identify a matching slope. Yet vacancies respond to productivity and outside options, measurement conventions can change, and unobserved matching efficiency can move with tightness. A regression slope therefore needs an explicit error model, identifying variation and timing argument. Flow observations must handle repeated within-period transitions; nonstationary observations require u′. The permanent-shock example shows an exact stationary-inversion error even without measurement noise.

Even a fitted wage does not by itself identify bargaining power: an omitted home benefit, firm productivity, recruiting cost or wage-setting institution can offset a different η. A parameter declared by calibration is an assumption unless the stated data and restrictions distinguish it. To evaluate a productivity mechanism, first hold the estimation sample and shock definition fixed, estimate or calibrate parameters transparently, and test predicted flow and wage responses on withheld moments with uncertainty. No such empirical exercise has been performed by the synthetic examples.

The model assumes workers can absorb employment risk in a linear utility scale. Incomplete markets changes that interpretation: borrowing limits and consumption risk can make outside values distribution-dependent. The next chapter’s nominal rigidities introduce different wage/price-setting restrictions; do not combine them with instant Nash renegotiation without rebuilding the equilibrium. Participation, skill mismatch and wage dispersion likewise need extra states and decisions.

7. Original exercises and complete solutions

  1. Starting from the short-interval hazard definition, derive the aggregate unemployment equation and its solution for constant f,s. Derive both endpoint worker transition probabilities over Δ, allowing repeated switches. Reconstruct Worked case 1 and explain why 1−exp(−fΔ) is not generally the endpoint employment probability.
  2. Derive all four stationary value equations from a first-dt comparison. State ownership and financing assumptions, and derive the Nash surplus shares while holding the correct outside values fixed. Prove the wage equation and show that a zero-value vacancy still incurs positive costs.
  3. Prove that the active stationary equilibrium exists uniquely for the stated primitive domain and y>b. Construct every stock, value and flow from the root and verify the original equations. Handle y=b and y<b without evaluating q(0). Reconstruct all baseline quantities and reconcile aggregate real surplus.
  4. Derive the signs of dθ/dy, dθ/db, dθ/dκ, dθ/dr, dθ/ds, dθ/dA and dθ/dη. At the baseline compute dθ/dy, df/dy, du*/dy and dw/dy. Explain why the sign of a market comparative static is not a causal estimate.
  5. Reconstruct the permanent productivity shock, including the immediate vacancy jump, the half-gap date’s unemployment, matches and derivative, and the false stationary estimate of f. Calculate exact discounted recruiting cost and a sufficient owned reserve. Explain which timing assumptions justify the jump to new market values and which future-shock changes would invalidate it.
  6. Derive the planner’s affine candidate and prove its global discounted optimality over every admissible time-varying tightness path using a finite-T inequality and a vanishing remainder. State the objective, feasibility, financing and initial-state comparison. Prove uniqueness almost everywhere and the exact Hosios equivalence within this model.
  7. Reconstruct the low-bargaining equilibrium and its fixed-policy evaluation. Compare it with the planner from u0=1/11, not from each policy’s own steady state. Explain how it has lower stationary unemployment but worse discounted surplus, and why the comparison is not automatically a Pareto improvement.
  8. For α=1/2 write a general formula for the positive equilibrium root in x=√θ. At the baseline audit candidate 121/100: compute H at that candidate, the residual-certified θ error and the actual error. Derive the bisection bracket guarantee, identify its domain, and explain what changes when y≤b.
  9. The baseline observations reveal u,v,s,w and the listed r,κ,y,b. Give two different matching elasticities with the same observed equilibrium, one satisfying Hosios and the other not. Explain what extra restrictions and variation could identify the elasticity. Separately derive the stationary Beveridge curve v(u), and explain why a moving observed pair need not lie on it.
  10. Referee this fictional report: “We inserted an annual job-finding rate of two as a transition probability. Entry has zero value, so recruiting requires no financing. The model fits one steady unemployment observation, so its bargaining and matching parameters are identified. The policy with the smallest steady unemployment rate is welfare optimal. When b is an insurance benefit, raising it creates b units of new aggregate output per unemployed worker.” Supply a precise correction and a relevant chapter witness for each claim. Give the additional evidence or model accounting each corrected claim requires.
Complete solutions and research-critique rubric

  1. Over dt, a mass s(1−u)dt leaves employment and fu dt leaves unemployment, up to o(dt); dividing the net change gives u′=s−(s+f)u. The integrating factor gives u(t)=s/(s+f)+[u0−s/(s+f)]exp(−(s+f)t). It is a convex combination of u0 and the stationary share, proving feasibility and convergence. For an initially unemployed worker substitute u0=1 and subtract from one to obtain f(1−exp(−(s+f)Δ))/(s+f). For an initially employed worker substitute u0=0 to obtain s(1−exp(−(s+f)Δ))/(s+f). With f=1,s=1/10 and exponential factor 1/2 these are 5/11 and 1/22; the two-state invariant unemployment share is (1/22)/(5/11+1/22)=1/11. The first-finding probability 1−exp(−fΔ) disregards possible separations after finding. It equals endpoint employment only if such departures are excluded, for example s=0 in this model.

  2. For unemployment, U=b dt+(1−r dt)[(1−f dt)U+f dt E]+o(dt); subtracting U and dividing gives rU=b+f(E−U). The identical expansion gives rE=w+s(U−E), rV=−κ+q(J−V) and rJ=y−w+s(V−J). These values concern discounted flows, with finite hazard and constant bounded flows; the expected discounted terminal-value argument establishes their interpretation. Owners finance recruiting and own firm claims; workers earn wages. Frictionless financing is an explicit assumption, and κ is still paid.

    At positive entry V=0. A pair takes U fixed, so X=(w−rU)/(r+s), J=(y−w)/(r+s), and S=X+J=(y−rU)/(r+s) is fixed in the bargain. Strict concavity of ηlog X+(1−η)log(S−X) gives X=ηS and J=(1−η)S. Since rU=b+fηS, the total-surplus identity becomes (r+s+ηf)S=y−b. Then w=b+η(r+s+f)S=ηy+(1−η)b+η(1−η)fS; κ=q(1−η)S and θq=f give the wage formula. In the baseline κ=1/2 while V=0 and J=1/2: zero entry value balances the expected cost and return rather than erasing either.

  3. For y>b, H starts strictly negative, is continuous, is unbounded above and is strictly increasing on θ>0, so exactly one positive root exists. Construct q,f and S=(y−b)/(r+s+ηf), then X=ηS,J=(1−η)S,U=(b+fX)/r,E=U+X,w=b+(r+s+f)X. The root implies κ=qJ; these definitions give rU,rE,rJ and rV=0 exactly. They also give w−b>0, y−w>0, u=s/(s+f)∈(0,1), v=θu and m=fu=s(1−u). Every active equilibrium reverses these algebraic steps, proving completeness. Nonentry when y>b fails the stated limiting-entry test: the prospective vacancy value is positive for sufficiently large finite q, as derived in Section 3.

    At y≤b, H has no positive root. In the inactive stationary market U=b/r. A potential agreement would require w≥b for the worker and w≤y for the firm. At strict inequality no such wage exists; at equality total surplus is zero and cannot cover a positive vacancy cost. Thus u=1,v=0 is the inactive outcome, without using q(0). Baseline x=√θ solves 5x²+2x−7=0 and x=1; rates, values and stocks are those in Worked case 2. Consolidation gives (9/10)(10/11)+(1/5)(1/11)−(1/2)(1/11)=87/110, and uU+(1−u)(E+J)=87/11. The flow equals r times the stationary value; wages appear once as receipts and once as payments and cancel.

  4. At a root let D=H′=κ[(r+s)αθ^(α−1)/A+η]>0. Differentiating gives θ_y=(1−η)/D, θ_b=−(1−η)/D, θ_κ=−[(r+s)θ^α/A+ηθ]/D, θ_r=θ_s=−κθ^α/(AD), θ_A=κ(r+s)θ^α/(A²D), and θ_η=−[κθ+y−b]/D. All claimed signs follow from the declared interior domain. For productivity, f_y=(1−α)f θ_y/θ, u_y=−s f_y/(s+f)², and w_y=η+ηκθ_y.

    At the baseline D=3/10, so (θ_y,f_y,u_y,w_y)=(5/3,5/6,-25/363,11/12). These derivatives hold other primitives and wage institutions fixed. Actual productivity variation may be correlated with separations, matching efficiency, worker composition or policy; measurement and an identification design would be needed to interpret an observed response causally.

  5. With y=13/5, H in x=√θ becomes (1/4)x²+(1/10)x−6/5=0, so x=2 and θ=4. Then f=2,q=1/2,S=2,X=1,J=1,w=12/5,U=22,E=23,u*=1/21. Initially u remains 1/11 and v=4/11. The transition equation has decay rate 21/10; at t=10log2/21 the gap halves, so u=16/231,v=64/231,m=32/231 and u′=s−(s+f)u=−1/22. Imposing u′=0 instead would return (1/10)(215/16)=43/32. Restoring −u′/u adds the missing 21/32 and gives two.

    The recruiting present value is κθ[u*/r+(u0−u*)/(r+s+f)]=2[(1/21)/(1/10)+(1/11−1/21)/(11/5)]=120/121. Reserve (κ·4/11)/r=20/11 earns enough to cover every date’s recruiting flow. It is sufficient rather than minimal and is owned before recruitment. Immediate value changes use unanticipated permanent news, instant renegotiation, free vacancy adjustment and no aggregate financing constraint. An anticipated reversal or recurrent shock requires continuation-value terms; merely substituting today’s y in a steady formula omits them.

  6. Take the planner objective and dynamics exactly as stated, from a common u0. For W=a−Du, reward plus its state derivative is y−sD+u[b−y+sD−κθ+Df]. For D>0, strict concavity and the two endpoint slope/value limits make g(θ)=Df−κθ attain its unique global maximum at κ=(1−α)qD. Coefficient matching requires ra=y−sD and (r+s+f)D=y−b+κθ; combining gives (r+s+αf)D=y−b and the unique positive planner root. This constructs the candidate without assuming an HJB solution exists.

    The global maximization inequality rW≥reward+W′u′ holds pointwise. Multiply by exp(−rt), use d[exp(−rt)W(u(t))]/dt=exp(−rt)[W′u′−rW], integrate through finite T and rearrange. Bounded W on [0,1] makes the terminal remainder vanish. Feasible objective limits exist because production/home flows are bounded and the declared controls have finite discounted costs; infinite costs are dominated. Constant θP attains equality and is itself feasible, so it maximizes the full discounted objective. Positive s makes u(t)>0 for t>0, and a nonzero-measure departure from θP creates a strictly positive integrated gap by strict concavity, proving uniqueness almost everywhere.

    Setting η=α makes market and planner equations identical. Conversely the market equation solves uniquely for η at a given θ via the displayed positive denominator; hence matching θP requires η=α. The proof includes owners and real recruiting costs and uses b as real outside utility. It compares policies from the same initial state and does not assert individual gains or an insurance-transfer resource benefit.

  7. At η=1/3 the positive solution of 5x²+3x−14=0 is 7/5, giving θ=49/25,f=7/5,u*=1/15. Free entry gives J=κ/q=7/10; S=J/(2/3)=21/20, and the wage formula yields 19/25. For a fixed rule, coefficient matching without maximizing gives Dθ=(y−b+κθ)/(r+s+f), aθ=(y−sDθ)/r. Here these are 21/20 and 159/20. The bounded state remainder proves Wθ is the attained value of that rule.

    At u0=1/11, the planner value is 8−1/11=87/11, while the distorted value is 159/20−21/220=432/55, a loss 3/55. Its stationary unemployment 1/15 is smaller, but excessive recruiting consumes resources. The planner’s objective balances that cost against employment production and lost home utility. The wage change redistributes bargaining rents; aggregate gain does not compensate each loser automatically. A Pareto claim would require an explicit feasible transfer scheme and participation accounting.

  8. Put d=r+s and C=(1−η)(y−b). Then κηx²+(κd/A)x−C=0. For C>0 its roots have opposite signs and the positive root is [−κd/A+sqrt((κd/A)²+4κηC)]/(2κη), with θ=x². At the baseline θhat=121/100 has xhat=11/10. Direct substitution gives (H(θhat),certified error,actual error)=(1/16,1/4,21/100), since κη=1/4. The true root is one, so actual error 21/100 is below the valid but loose bound 1/4.

    A bracket [L,R] with H(L)≤0≤H(R) retains its root when the midpoint replaces the endpoint with the same strict sign. The interval width halves per step; the final midpoint is within width/2 of the root. Doubling an upper endpoint eventually brackets because H→infinity. This root algorithm assumes y>b and positive κ,A,r,s with interior α,η. At y≤b there is no positive root to locate: return the separately verified inactive regime, rather than divide by q(0) or keep iterating for an absent positive solution.

  9. Both α=1/2 and α=1/3 with A=1 produce f=q=1 at θ=1. Keep η=1/2 and the other baseline primitives; the same H root, wage, values and unemployment result because θ^α=1. Only the first satisfies η=α. Thus a single fitted steady state does not identify the matching elasticity or establish efficiency. Given independently known κ,r,s,y,b the entry equation at θ=1 does identify η=1/2, but the listed observation does not identify α. If those other primitives are estimated or mismeasured, even that conditional η inference can fail.

    From s(1−u)=Au^αv^(1−α), solve v=[s/A]^(1/(1−α))(1−u)^(1/(1−α))u^(−α/(1−α)) for 0<u<1. Its log derivative is −1/[(1−α)(1−u)]−α/[(1−α)u]<0. Stable matching efficiency and credible independent tightness variation could identify the slope in log f; endogenous efficiency and measurement errors require extra restrictions/instruments/data. A nonstationary observation instead obeys s(1−u)−Au^αv^(1−α)=u′, so it need not lie on the stationary curve. The shock’s half-gap point supplies an exact counterexample.

  10. Benchmark critique. (1) A hazard of two has inverse-time units; the endpoint transition uses the exponential two-state formula and remains at most one. Specify sampling interval and repeated-transition treatment before estimating probabilities. (2) V=0 equates expected returns with positive recruiting costs; κ=1/2 in the baseline. State who owns the recruiting reserve or which enforceable financing arrangement pays it, then include costs once in consolidated resources. (3) Baseline α=1/2 and α=1/3 are observationally equivalent at θ=f=1, although they imply different efficiency conclusions. Identify the parameter-to-moment mapping, maintained cost/outside-option data and credible variation rather than labeling a fit as identification. (4) η=1/3 lowers stationary u to 1/15 but loses 3/55 in discounted surplus from u0=1/11. Specify the planner objective, matching constraints, financing and common initial state; an individual-gain claim also needs distributional accounting. (5) Insurance cash received by an unemployed worker is paid by someone else; the transfer cancels in aggregate output. Separate leisure/home production from transfers, specify taxes and any financing distortions, and rederive both private incentives and the social objective.

    Ten-point rubric. For each of the five claims award one point for a concrete correct contradiction or account and one for the stated replacement conditions/evidence. A theorem name or policy preference without the mechanism earns no correction point. Accept alternative examples that preserve the specified model or explicitly identify a changed assumption. Neither endorsement nor rejection of a policy receives automatic credit.

8. Explain and retain the model

Teach-back. Explain in two minutes why an individual firm treats q as given while aggregate vacancies determine it; why the wage is not simply a fixed share of output; why a stationary unemployment identity does not determine entry; and why minimizing unemployment differs from maximizing surplus.

Teach-back benchmark

An atomistic firm takes the ratio of market vacancies to searchers as fixed; free entry changes that ratio for the market as a whole. Pair bargaining splits the value gain relative to U and V, so the worker outside option includes future job opportunities and the equilibrium wage contains ηκθ. Flow balance determines u only after entry determines f. The planner values additional production and lost home utility while paying real recruiting costs. The low-worker-share example produces more recruiting and less unemployment but lower discounted surplus from the same starting point.

Delayed retention. After two days rederive κ=qJ, the scalar root equation and the exact unemployment transition; recompute baseline wage and both worker values without using the example. After two weeks prove the finite-T planner verification, identify which matching elasticity belongs in Hosios, and explain why one steady observation cannot establish efficiency.

Retention answers

Free entry sets V=0 in rV=−κ+q(J−V), giving κ=qJ. Combining J=(1−η)(y−b)/(r+s+ηf), q=Aθ^(−α) and f=θq gives H(θ)=0. Constant hazards imply u(t)=s/(s+f)+[u0−s/(s+f)]exp(−(s+f)t). Baseline S=1, X=J=1/2, U=(1/5+1/2)/(1/10)=7, E=15/2 and w=b+(r+s+f)X=4/5.

For W=a−Du, maximize Df−κθ globally, obtain the planner coefficients, integrate the Bellman inequality with the exp(−rt) factor and use bounded W to remove the endpoint. The relevant elasticity is α with respect to unemployment, so η=α, not 1−α. At θ=f=1, A=1 fits every α; the same observed equilibrium can therefore be efficient under one matching technology and inefficient under another. This conclusion is about identification, not a statement that every parameterization fits additional data.

Method source and scope

Daron Acemoglu, MIT 14.661, Lectures 11–13: Search, Matching and Unemployment, December 5, 7 and 12, 2017 supplies the continuous-time matching, pair-specific bargaining, entry and constrained-efficiency method context. The source record distinguishes the earlier accepted inspection from the present official-body inspection. This chapter supplies its own complete existence and discounted planner verification, excludes the source’s physical-capital extensions, and uses original cases and exercises. No historical empirical assertion, unrestricted efficiency theorem or full-course review is imported. Direct derivations, not imperfectly extracted source displays, determine the equations printed here.
